title: Barossa Valley
description: Australia's most famous region: rich Shiraz from some of the oldest vines in the world.
L: A warm valley north of Adelaide

The Barossa Valley lies about 60 km north-east of Adelaide, in South Australia. The valley floor is about 250 to 300 m; the hills to the east rise into the cooler Eden Valley. Together they form the Barossa zone. The Barossa Valley has about 13,000 hectares of vines. Soils range from sand to red-brown clay and ironstone.

The Barossa Valley has a warm, dry Mediterranean climate: hot summers, often over 35 degrees, and cool, wet winters. Most rain falls in winter. Many old vines are dry-grown, without irrigation, their deep roots finding water. Warmth gives ripe, full-bodied reds.
What type of climate does the Barossa Valley have?

In the 1840s, Lutheran settlers from Silesia, then in Prussia, now Poland, settled the Barossa, fleeing religious persecution. They brought farming skills, German food traditions like mettwurst and bienenstich, and Lutheran churches. Many wine families, like Henschke, Hentschke, and Seppelt, have German roots. The heritage is still visible today.
The Barossa was settled by Lutherans from Silesia in the 1840s.
The Barossa lies north-east of Adelaide
Its warm, dry climate gives ripe reds; old vines are dry-grown
Silesian settlers shaped its culture from the 1840s

Shiraz, Syrah, is the Barossa's signature, about half of the vineyards. It gives full-bodied, ripe wines with blackberry, plum, chocolate, liquorice and spice, often 14.5 to 15% alcohol, with soft, ripe tannins. Traditional examples use American oak, adding vanilla and coconut. Penfolds Grange, first made in 1951, often includes Barossa Shiraz.
Rich Shiraz, about half the vines

Grenache, often from old bush vines, gives red fruit and spice. Mourvèdre, called Mataro locally, adds tannin and savoury notes. Blends of Grenache, Shiraz and Mourvèdre, GSM, are a Barossa classic. Cabernet Sauvignon and Semillon also grow. Eden Valley adds Riesling.

Explain why the Barossa has old vines

South Australia has never had phylloxera, thanks to strict quarantine laws. So the Barossa has some of the world's oldest producing vines, ungrafted, on their own roots. Some Shiraz vines were planted in the 1840s, like at Langmeil's Freedom vineyard and Turkey Flat; Grenache and Mourvèdre vines are similarly old.

In 2009, the Barossa created the Old Vine Charter to register and protect old vineyards. It has four levels: Old Vine, at least 35 years; Survivor Vine, 70 years; Centenarian Vine, 100 years; and Ancestor Vine, 125 years or more. Producers can show these on labels.
Order the Barossa Old Vine Charter levels from youngest to oldest.

Old vines have deep roots that find water in drought, so many are dry-grown. They give low yields of small, concentrated berries, with balance and complexity. They're also a living record of 19th century viticulture, and valuable genetic material, since Europe's original vines were mostly lost to phylloxera.
Why does the Barossa have such old vines?
South Australia is phylloxera-free, so old vines survive
The Old Vine Charter registers vines from 35 to 125 years

Compare it with the Barossa Valley

Eden Valley lies in the hills east of the Barossa Valley, at about 400 to 600 m. It's cooler, windier and wetter, with granite and schist soils. It's part of the Barossa zone but a separate GI. Its wines are fresher and more elegant than the valley floor's.

Eden Valley is famous for dry Riesling: lime, lemon and floral when young, developing toast and honey with age. Its Shiraz is more peppery and elegant than Barossa Valley Shiraz. Henschke's Hill of Grace, from Shiraz vines planted around 1860, is one of Australia's most famous wines.
What makes Eden Valley cooler than the Barossa Valley?
Hill of Grace takes its name from the Lutheran church across the road, Gnadenberg, meaning hill of grace.
Eden Valley is cool and hilly.
Eden Valley is higher and cooler, in the eastern hills
It's famous for dry Riesling and elegant Shiraz

Reading the Barossa and eating with it

Australian labels show the grape, the GI, like Barossa Valley or Eden Valley, and the vintage, each at least 85%. Blends list grapes in order of share, like GSM or Shiraz Cabernet. The Barossa zone covers both valleys. Old Vine Charter levels may appear. Wines are often sealed with screw caps.

Barossa Shiraz suits barbecued meat, lamb, beef, kangaroo and rich stews. Its ripe fruit handles sweet, smoky sauces. GSM suits roast lamb and game. Eden Valley Riesling suits seafood, Asian dishes and salads. Barossa's German heritage dishes, like mettwurst, a smoked sausage, suit Shiraz too. Serve Shiraz at 16 to 18 degrees.
